messages.subject: point transect: radial v's perpendicular distances
messages.subject_clean: point transect: radial v's perpendicular distances
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance-sampling list,

I have avian point transect data that was collected using perpendicular
distance categories.  From what I have read from the 1993 edition of Intro.
to Distance Sampling, it appears that only radial distances are used for
point transects, whereas line transects can use either radial or
perpendicular distances.  Can perpendicular distance categories be used for
analyzing point transect data in DISTANCE?

Thanks,
Mike Baldwin
graduate student
mba...@lsu.edu

messages.subject: Re: point transect: radial v's perpendicular distances
messages.subject_clean: point transect: radial v's perpendicular distances
messages.body_plain:
> > I have avian point transect data that was collected using perpendicular
> > distance categories.  From what I have read from the 1993 edition of Intro.
> > to Distance Sampling, it appears that only radial distances are used for
> > point transects, whereas line transects can use either radial or
> > perpendicular distances.  Can perpendicular distance categories be used for
> > analyzing point transect data in DISTANCE?

For point transects, there is only one detection distance.  For line
transects, you can have either the distance of the detected animal from
the observer (the radial distance) or its shortest distance to the line
(the perpendicular distance).  For points, distance to the observer and
distance to the point are the same thing.  This distance is termed the
radial distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Automatic model selection vs AIC
messages.body_plain:
> > I am a Distance learner analyising bird data. I have tried using AIC to select the best fit model for my data, but the models that the program chooses have incredible standard errors compared to those given by Half-normal/Cosine which is automatically chosen by the program. What could be the problem?

If your data are spiked, and AIC selects a hazard-rate model, it is
probably fitting that spike, and fitting a detection function that falls
implausibly quickly.  You should examine your data, and try to understand
what feature of the data is causing a problem.  e.g. were many of your
distances rounded to zero?  Or were there lots of values very close to
zero?  If you are happy that your data are sufficiently reliable for
analysis, then exclude the hazard-rate model from the set you consider.

Steve Buckland

Abundance Using Aerial Line Transect Surveys" in pdf format.  The manual

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/pronghorn.html

It is also linked from the Distance home page
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Hope it's of use to some of you, and thanks to Rich for making it available.

messages.subject_clean: Raw data groupings vs Distance groupings
messages.body_plain:
Please look in the online help index under "Interval data" or "Grouped data"
to find out how to tell distance your data were collected in intervals.  If
you don't tell Distance the data were collected in intervals, it assumes they
are "exact" and gives 3 histogram plots by default, as described in the online
help, Chapter 8 | Output from CDS Analyses | CDS Results Details Listing.
There is more information about this in the Appendix - Program Reference under
Data Filter and Model Definition.

Please make sure you have read the online manual thoroughly before posting to
the list.  Thanks,

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: SQL Selection Criteria
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am attempting to estimate grassland bird densities in experimental
pastures in order to evaluate the effects of a new restoration technique.
I hope to eventually compare densities among pastures. I have two
replicate pastures per treatment, and would ultimately like to test models
that combine data from replicates (so that I can also look for differences
in density across treatments, not just by pasture). I have assigned
pasture to the stratum level, but cannot seem to figure out the SQL code
to filter out all but two pastures at once in the selection criteria
dialogue. Not having much luck with the online manual. Is this type of
filter even possible? Any suggestions?

Tracey Johnson
Graduate Research Assistant
Division of Biology
Kansas State University
Manhattan, KS 66502
tra...@ksu.edu

messages.subject: Re: SQL Selection Criteria
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tracey, List,

There are a few ways to set up a project to achieve your goals (including
the way you have done it), depending on at what level you're going to
estimate the detection function.

If you have a fairly large sample size of observations, then you may decide
a priori that you're not going to pool across treatments for estimating the
detection function -- i.e., that you're either going to estimate a separate
detection function for each pasture, or that you're going to pool the two
pastures in treatment 1 and estimate one detection function, and pool the
two pastures in treatment 2 and estimate another.

In this case, one option would be to set the two treatments up as separate
Distance projects.  You'd then estimate density separately in each project
and use the stuff in section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. 2001 to compare
densities.

Another option for this case is to do what you have done -- put all the data
in one project and make pasture the stratum.  Then use data selection to
pull out only the two pastures for treatment 1 for one set of analyses, and
another data selection to pull out the two pastures for treatment 2.  How
exactly to do this?  Let's say pastures for treatment 1 have ID 1 and 2.
Then in Data Filter | Data selection, you click on the "+" button on the
right hand side, under "Layer type" you'd choose Stratum and under
"Selection criteria" you'd write (ID=1) OR (ID=2).  An alternative would be
if the two pastures had Label fields "Pasture 1" and "Pasture 2" you could
put for "Selection criteria"  (Label='Pasture 1') OR (Label='Pasture 2').  A
third alternative would be that you could create a new field in the stratum
layer,and call it "Treatment".  You'd then put, say, "1" in that field for
pastures in treatment 1, and "2" for pastures in treatment 2.  Then your
selection criterion would be Treatment=1.  Hope this makes sense - if not,
send me a copy of your project and I'll show you.

In both of the above cases, to get an estimate of density by pasture, you
ask for density by stratum.

You might also want to investigate pooling the detection function across
treatments - perhaps because you have too small a sample size to do
otherwise, or perhaps because you want to try pooling across treatments, and
try estimating a separate detection function for each treatment, and let AIC
(or some other criterion) tell you which is preferable.  If you do decide to
pool across treatments, then you are assuming the probability of detection
is the same for both treatments, and you may as well compare mean counts
between pastures rather than densities.  Life would get a bit more
complicated if your birds occured in clusters rather than as individuals and
you had evidence if size bias, but I'll ignore this.

You might also want to investigate an intermediate route, which is to try
pasture (or treatment) as a factor covariate using the MCDS engine.  This
allows detection probability to vary by pasture (or treatment), but only the
scale of the function varies -- the shape is the same between pastures -- it
takes less parameters so may work better for small sample sizes.  For more
on this, see the MCDS chapter of the Advanced Distance Sampling book, and
also chapter 9 of the online manual.  In this case comparing densities
between treatments is no longer straightforward as the pastures are no
longer independent (they share the shape part of the detection function).
As usual, you have a few options - this time they depend on whether you want
to view your two replicate pastures as a sample of all possible pastures
that could have been given the treatment (random effect) or you want to
restrict your inferences to just the observed differences in the four
pastures you sampled (fixed effect).  In the former case, you could consider
pooling the data for all points in each pasture and making pasture the
"sample" and treatment the stratum.  In the latter case, you could consider
keeping point within pasture as the sample, and bootstrapping by sample to
estimate variance.  You'd keep the density estimates in each stratum
(pasture) in each bootstrap replicate (you can do this in Distance by asking
it to save the bootstrap file), and then calculate the difference between
treatment and control for each bootstrap replicate, and use these to get
mean difference and confidence limits on the difference.  If you use either
of these approaches for the MCDS analysis, you'd want to use the same
approach in the previous analyses for consistency.

This is a lot to pack into one email, so you may want to take some of these
issues up with your local statistician.  Nonetheless, hope it's helped
some...

 - Len

--

Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
